name: Resin infiltration (ICON)

lead: Resin infiltration fills the porous enamel of early lesions with a thin resin. Dentists use it for white spots after braces and some fluorosis or hypomineralisation marks.
It has randomised trials and many registered studies behind it.

paras: Low-viscosity resin penetrates demineralised enamel, stabilising it and changing its light scattering so spots look closer to surrounding enamel.
The sources reviewed do not list specific harms. Long-term cosmetic results were not summarised, and one registered fluorosis follow-up was withdrawn.

lead: Resin infiltration is a micro-invasive dental treatment in which a low-viscosity resin is infiltrated into porous, demineralised enamel to arrest early lesions and, as a cosmetic effect, mask white spots; Icon is the best-known commercial product. An encyclopedia article on tooth decay describes resin infiltration as a micro-invasive intervention shown to slow progression of proximal decay.[1]

In appearance contexts it is discussed for white spot lesions after braces and for opacities from fluorosis or molar incisor hypomineralisation. Published case reports and randomised trials exist, and many trials are registered.[2][3]
infobox: White spot lesions, early caries, some hypomineralised enamel

paras: Orthodontic patients show higher rates of white spot lesions around fixed appliances, and resin infiltration is among the managements discussed. A clinical report described masking labial white spots by resin infiltration. Trials also cover fluorosis stains, with or without bleaching,[4] and molar incisor hypomineralisation incisors.[5]

Published studies include a 2007 paper on resin infiltration of natural caries lesions[2] and a 2010 randomised efficacy trial of resin infiltration of caries lesions.[3] A systematic review and network meta-analysis of nonrestorative caries treatments in 2019 included infiltration among the options.[6] Registered trials examine aesthetic performance on enamel lesions,[7] 80 patients with fluorosis stains,[4] comparison with microabrasion,[8] and pediatric hypomineralisation.[5] Outcome data from these registrations were not available in the sources.
Registered fluorosis follow-up of Icon (NCT02925780) was withdrawn.[9] Long-term colour stability data are not summarised in the sources reviewed.
